title: Microprocessors & ARM Architecture
blurb: Microprocessor fundamentals, system components, memory hierarchy, performance, RISC, ARM architecture, registers, modes, CPSR, and endianness.
description: An engineering-focused microprocessors and ARM architecture course covering processor fundamentals, ARM architecture, memory, I/O, and practical low-level programming.

lessons.title: Microprocessor fundamentals & the CPU
objectives: Explain the CPU's role in a computer
lessons.explanation: A microprocessor is a computer's CPU implemented on a single integrated circuit. It fetches and executes instructions, performs arithmetic and logical work, and coordinates data movement with memory and I/O. Modern processors contain very large numbers of transistors connected to implement datapaths, control logic, caches, and other structures.
examples:
pc = 0x00001000  # Program counter holds next instruction address
instruction = 0xE2801005  # Fetched instruction (ADD r1, r0, #5)
opcode = (instruction >> 21) & 0xF  # Decode opcode bits 24:21
print(hex(pc), opcode)  # Execute and log operation
commonMistakes: Treating a microprocessor as the entire computer rather than the CPU that works with memory and I/O.
lessons.explain: A microprocessor is a computer's CPU implemented on a single integrated circuit. It fetches and executes instructions, performs arithmetic and logical work, and coordinates data movement with memory and I/O. lessons.title: From early computers to modern microprocessors
objectives: Connect transistor scaling to processor capability
lessons.explanation: Processor development moved from large vacuum-tube systems to transistors, integrated circuits, and then complete CPUs on a chip. Integration reduced size and cost while allowing much larger transistor counts and more capable processors.
examples:
# Scaling from Intel 4004 to modern 64-bit ARM
bus_widths = [4, 8, 16, 32, 64]  # Address bus bit widths
# Iterate over bus widths to calculate capacity
for bits in bus_widths:
    addressable_bytes = 1 << bits  # 2^N bytes total addressable address space
    print(bits, addressable_bytes)  # Output bit width and byte capacity
commonMistakes: Memorizing dates without understanding the architectural change each technology made possible.
lessons.explain: Processor development moved from large vacuum-tube systems to transistors, integrated circuits, and then complete CPUs on a chip. Integration reduced size and cost while allowing much larger transistor counts and more capable processors.

lessons.title: Computer components, microprocessors, microcontrollers & SoCs
objectives: Distinguish a microprocessor from a microcontroller
lessons.explanation: A computer system combines the processor with memory and I/O support. Cache keeps frequently needed data close to the CPU, DRAM provides larger working memory, and platform logic connects components and peripherals. A microcontroller integrates a CPU with memory and peripherals, while a system-on-chip integrates still more system functions.
examples:
sram_base = 0x40000000  # On-chip SRAM starting address
flash_base = 0x00000000  # On-chip Flash starting address
gpio_base = 0xE0028000  # Memory-mapped GPIO peripheral base
print(hex(flash_base), hex(sram_base), hex(gpio_base))  # Output memory regions
commonMistakes: Assuming microprocessors, microcontrollers, and SoCs differ only in speed rather than in integration and intended use.
lessons.explain: A computer system combines the processor with memory and I/O support. A microcontroller integrates a CPU with memory and peripherals, while a system-on-chip integrates still more system functions.

lessons.title: Memory hierarchy & cache evolution
objectives: Describe the trend toward on-chip caches
lessons.explanation: Memory is organized as a hierarchy because no single technology is simultaneously the fastest, largest, and cheapest. Registers are closest to execution, then caches, then main memory. Processor history moved caches from the motherboard toward on-die L1, L2, and L3 levels.
examples:
# Memory hierarchy levels with latency
hierarchy = [("Registers", 1), ("L1 Cache", 4), ("L2 Cache", 12), ("DRAM", 120)]  # Level latencies
# Iterate across memory hierarchy
for name, latency in hierarchy:
    print(name, latency)  # Print level name and access cycle latency
commonMistakes: Thinking every memory access costs the same amount of time.

lessons.title: Architecture vs microarchitecture
objectives: Explain how two processors can share an ISA
lessons.explanation: Architecture defines the programmer-visible contract, including instructions, registers, data types, and behavior. Microarchitecture is how a particular processor implements that contract. Two processors can execute the same instruction set while using different caches, pipelines, issue widths, or out-of-order machinery.
examples:
instructions = 100  # Total instructions in workload
pipeline_cycles = 5 + (instructions - 1)  # 5-cycle fill latency + 1 cycle per subsequent instruction
print(instructions, pipeline_cycles)  # Output instruction count and cycle total
commonMistakes: Using 'architecture' and 'microarchitecture' as interchangeable words.

Two processors can execute the same instruction set while using different caches, pipelines, issue widths, or out-of-order machinery.

lessons.title: Processor performance: time, clock rate & IPC
objectives: Use execution time as the primary performance measure
Relate IPC/CPI and clock rate to performance
Explain why deeper pipelines have trade-offs
lessons.explanation: Processor performance is fundamentally about how long a workload takes. Clock frequency affects cycles per second, while IPC describes how much instruction work completes per cycle. Pipelining can raise frequency, dependencies and stalls reduce IPC, and superscalar or out-of-order execution can expose more parallel work.
examples:
instr_count = 1_000_000  # Total dynamic instruction count
cpi = 1.25  # Average cycles per instruction
clock_mhz = 50.0  # Clock frequency in MHz
exec_time_sec = (instr_count * cpi) / (clock_mhz * 1e6)  # Compute execution time
print(exec_time_sec)  # Output total duration in seconds
commonMistakes: Assuming a higher clock rate automatically means a faster processor for every program.
lessons.explain: Processor performance is fundamentally about how long a workload takes. Clock frequency affects cycles per second, while IPC describes how much instruction work completes per cycle. Pipelining can raise frequency, dependencies and stalls reduce IPC, and superscalar or out-of-order execution can expose more parallel work.

lessons.title: RISC principles & ARM architecture
objectives: Connect ARM design choices to embedded systems
lessons.explanation: Classic RISC uses a regular instruction set, a large register file, and explicit loads/stores for memory access. ARM follows this load-store model: data-processing instructions operate mainly on registers, while LDR/STR move data between registers and memory. This architectural model is the foundation for writing ARM assembly.
examples:
MOV r0, #0x4000 ; Set base address pointer
        MOV r1, #25 ; Set initial data value
        STR r1, [r0] ; Store value from register to memory
        LDR r2, [r0] ; Load value from memory into register
        ADD r2, r2, #5 ; Process data inside register file
stop    B stop ; Halt execution
commonMistakes: Interpreting RISC as 'every real instruction always completes in exactly one physical clock cycle.'
lessons.explain: Classic RISC uses a regular instruction set, a large register file, and explicit loads/stores for memory access. lessons.title: ARM instruction families, data sizes & execution state
objectives: Distinguish ARM and Thumb instruction encodings
lessons.explanation: ARM programming groups instructions into data movement, arithmetic, logical/bit-manipulation, shifts, comparisons, branches, and memory transfers. MOV/MVN move or invert values; ADD/SUB families perform arithmetic; AND/ORR/EOR/BIC manipulate bits; LSL/LSR/ASR/ROR shift Operand2. Classic ARM uses 32-bit instructions, while Thumb/Thumb-2 also use compact encodings. Halfword, word, and doubleword sizes are 16, 32, and 64 bits.
examples:
MOV r0, #0x2000 ; Set memory buffer pointer
        MOV r1, #0xFF ; Set byte value 255
        STRB r1, [r0] ; Store byte to memory
        MOV r2, #0x1234 ; Set 16-bit halfword value
        STRH r2, [r0, #2] ; Store halfword at offset 2
stop    B stop ; Halt execution
commonMistakes: Confusing instruction encoding size with the size of the data being processed.

Classic ARM uses 32-bit instructions, while Thumb/Thumb-2 also use compact encodings. Halfword, word, and doubleword sizes are 16, 32, and 64 bits.

lessons.title: ARM programmer model, registers, stack & subroutines
objectives: Explain the roles of SP, LR, and PC
Explain why some modes use banked registers
lessons.explanation: Classic ARM exposes general-purpose registers plus R13/SP, R14/LR, and R15/PC. SP tracks the runtime stack, BL saves a return address in LR, and BX LR can return to the caller. Calling conventions define how parameters and preserved registers are handled so separately written routines work together safely.
examples:
MOV r0, #10 ; Load general purpose register r0
        MOV r1, #20 ; Load general purpose register r1
        ADDS r2, r0, r1 ; Add r0 and r1 into r2 and update CPSR flags
        MOV r13, #0x1000 ; Initialize stack pointer SP
        MOV r14, #0x0000 ; Initialize link register LR
stop    B stop ; Halt execution
commonMistakes: Assuming every processor mode sees exactly the same physical SP, LR, and saved-status registers.

lessons.title: CPSR flags, processor modes, endianness & exceptions
objectives: Name the major classic ARM modes
lessons.explanation: CPSR contains the N, Z, C, and V condition flags along with execution-state, interrupt-mask, and mode bits. Comparison and flag-setting instructions update these flags for conditional execution. Classic ARM exceptions save status, switch to a privileged mode, and transfer control through a vector table; SVC requests a privileged software service. Endianness determines byte order in memory.
examples:
val = 0x12345678  # 32-bit test word
little_endian = [val & 0xFF, (val >> 8) & 0xFF, (val >> 16) & 0xFF, (val >> 24) & 0xFF]  # LSB first
big_endian = [(val >> 24) & 0xFF, (val >> 16) & 0xFF, (val >> 8) & 0xFF, val & 0xFF]  # MSB first
print(little_endian)  # Output little-endian byte array
print(big_endian)  # Output big-endian byte array
commonMistakes: Reading the ARM I and F CPSR bits as interrupt-enable bits; in classic ARM, a set mask bit masks/disables that interrupt.

labs.title: C++ and ARM Calling Convention Lab
labs.syllabusTopic: C++ comparison and mixed C++/assembly programming; AAPCS calling standard
labs.objective: Understand the ARM Architecture Procedure Call Standard (AAPCS): arguments passed in R0–R3, return value in R0, preserving callee-saved registers R4–R11 on the stack, and maintaining 8-byte stack alignment.
labs.problemStatement: Implement an AAPCS-compliant ARM assembly subroutine compute_polynomial that calculates a * x^2 + b * x + c, where a is in R0, b is in R1, c is in R2, and x is in R3. Preserve any non-volatile registers used and return the 32-bit integer result in R0.
labs.starterCode:
AREA PolyCode, CODE, READONLY ; Declare code section
        EXPORT compute_polynomial ; Export function name for C++ linkage
compute_polynomial ; Function entry point
        PUSH {r4, lr} ; Preserve callee-saved register r4 and link register
        MUL r4, r3, r3 ; Compute x^2 = x * x and store in r4
        MUL r0, r0, r4 ; Compute a * x^2 and store in r0
        MLA r0, r1, r3, r0 ; Compute (b * x) + (a * x^2) and store in r0
        ADD r0, r0, r2 ; Add constant c to accumulate final polynomial
        POP {r4, pc} ; Restore r4 and return by popping saved lr into pc
        END ; Mark end of assembly source
labs.expectedState: With inputs a=2, b=3, c=4, x=5: computes 2*(25) + 3*(5) + 4 = 69. R0 = 69 (0x00000045), R4 restored, SP balanced.
labs.boundaryCase: Large operand values (e.g. a=10000, x=1000) cause 32-bit integer multiplication overflow; callers passing 5 or more parameters must pass the 5th+ argument on the stack.
labs.hardwareNote: Browser tracer models 32-bit register and stack behavior; Keil/ARM7 hardware toolchains enforce 8-byte stack alignment at external boundaries and check AAPCS frame records.
labs.checkpoint: Verify that R4 is restored to its caller value and R0 contains 69 when tested with (2, 3, 4, 5).
labs.solutionCode:
AREA PolyCode, CODE, READONLY ; Declare code section
        EXPORT compute_polynomial ; Export function for C++ linkage
compute_polynomial ; Function entry point
        PUSH {r4-r5, lr} ; Save non-volatile registers r4, r5, and link register
        MUL r4, r3, r3 ; r4 = x * x (x^2)
        MUL r5, r0, r4 ; r5 = a * x^2
        MLA r0, r1, r3, r5 ; r0 = (b * x) + (a * x^2)
        ADD r0, r0, r2 ; r0 = (a * x^2 + b * x) + c
        POP {r4-r5, pc} ; Restore non-volatile registers and return
        END ; End of assembly file
labs.solutionExplanation: The subroutine follows AAPCS by receiving arguments in R0-R3, using non-volatile registers R4-R5 safely by saving them on entry and restoring them on exit, calculating the quadratic term, and returning the result in R0.

labs.title: Assembler Directives, Macros, Constants & Literal Pool Lab
labs.syllabusTopic: Assembler directives, macros, constants, and literal pools
labs.objective: Master assembler directives (AREA, ENTRY, END, ALIGN, SPACE, DCD, DCB), symbolic definitions (EQU, RN), macro definitions (MACRO, MEND), and literal pool placement (LTORG).
labs.problemStatement: Define symbolic bounds MIN_BOUND EQU 10 and MAX_BOUND EQU 100, register alias val RN 0, clamp val between bounds using conditional instructions, define an aligned lookup table with DCD, and place LTORG to dump literal constants.
labs.starterCode:
MIN_BOUND EQU 10 ; Define symbolic lower bound constant
MAX_BOUND EQU 100 ; Define symbolic upper bound constant
val RN 0 ; Create readable alias for register r0
tmp RN 1 ; Create readable alias for register r1

        AREA DirectivesLab, CODE, READONLY ; Declare read-only code area
        ENTRY ; Specify execution entry point
start ; Entry label
        MOV val, #5 ; Load test value below lower bound
        CMP val, #MIN_BOUND ; Compare test value against minimum bound
        MOVLT val, #MIN_BOUND ; Clamp to minimum if value is less than bound
        CMP val, #MAX_BOUND ; Compare test value against maximum bound
        MOVGT val, #MAX_BOUND ; Clamp to maximum if value exceeds bound
        LDR tmp, =0x12345678 ; Load 32-bit constant from literal pool
        LTORG ; Force assembler to dump literal pool here
stop B stop ; Infinite loop halting processor
        END ; End of assembly file
labs.expectedState: val (R0) is clamped from 5 to 10 (0x0000000A); tmp (R1) is loaded with 0x12345678; literal pool is placed immediately following LTORG.
labs.boundaryCase: Placing LDR rX, =constant more than 4095 bytes from literal pool without LTORG causes assembler error 'Literal pool out of range'; missing ALIGN 4 after DCB strings causes unaligned word reads.
labs.hardwareNote: Browser tracer resolves basic literals; Keil armasm evaluates multi-pass macro expansions, literal pool offsets, and flags unaligned section boundaries.
labs.checkpoint: Verify clamping for test inputs 5, 50, and 150, confirming R0 is bounded in [10, 100].
labs.solutionCode:
MIN_VAL EQU 10 ; Define minimum clamp value
MAX_VAL EQU 100 ; Define maximum clamp value
input RN 0 ; Input/output register alias
limit RN 1 ; Scratch limit register alias

        AREA ClampArea, CODE, READONLY ; Define code area
        ENTRY ; Set entry point
main ; Main entry label
        MOV input, #150 ; Load test value exceeding upper bound
        MOV limit, #MIN_VAL ; Load lower bound into scratch register
        CMP input, limit ; Check if input is below lower bound
        MOVLT input, limit ; Clamp input up to lower bound if less
        MOV limit, #MAX_VAL ; Load upper bound into scratch register
        CMP input, limit ; Check if input exceeds upper bound
        MOVGT input, limit ; Clamp input down to upper bound if greater
        LDR r2, =0xAABBCCDD ; Request 32-bit literal constant
        LTORG ; Place literal pool before code end
trap B trap ; Terminate in spin loop
        END ; End of assembly source
labs.solutionExplanation: EQU and RN define meaningful constants and register names; conditional moves perform branchless clamping; LTORG forces immediate allocation of literal table data.

labs.title: ARM Arithmetic & Data Movement Lab
labs.syllabusTopic: Data-processing instructions, 64-bit multiword arithmetic, barrel shifter
labs.objective: Implement multi-word (64-bit) addition and subtraction using ADDS, ADC, SUBS, SBC, and apply flexible second operand barrel shifter transformations (LSL, LSR, ASR, ROR).
labs.problemStatement: Implement a 64-bit unsigned addition: operand 1 in (R1:R0, where R1 is MSW, R0 is LSW) and operand 2 in (R3:R2, where R3 is MSW, R2 is LSW). Add lower words with ADDS to set carry, add upper words with ADC, and multiply the sum by 8 using barrel shifting.
labs.starterCode:
AREA MultiWord, CODE, READONLY ; Declare code area
        ENTRY ; Entry point
start ; Program start
        MOV r0, #0xFFFFFFFF ; Set lower 32 bits of operand 1
        MOV r1, #0x00000001 ; Set upper 32 bits of operand 1
        MOV r2, #0x00000001 ; Set lower 32 bits of operand 2
        MOV r3, #0x00000000 ; Set upper 32 bits of operand 2
        ADDS r0, r0, r2 ; Add lower words and update Carry flag (C=1)
        ADC r1, r1, r3 ; Add upper words including Carry flag
        MOV r4, r0, LSL #3 ; Shift lower sum left by 3 (multiply by 8)
stop B stop ; Halt execution
        END ; End of assembly source
labs.expectedState: Lower word R0 overflows to 0x00000000 with C=1; Upper word R1 becomes 1 + 0 + 1 = 2; 64-bit result is 0x0000000200000000.
labs.boundaryCase: 64-bit overflow occurs when MSW addition generates a carry out of bit 63; signed subtraction requires monitoring the V (overflow) flag.
labs.hardwareNote: Browser models 32-bit register updates and status flags; hardware ARM7 pipeline executes barrel shifter operations simultaneously with the ALU in a single cycle.
labs.checkpoint: Verify that lower word carry propagates into upper word, yielding R1:R0 = 0x00000002:0x00000000.
labs.solutionCode:
AREA Arith64, CODE, READONLY ; Code section
        ENTRY ; Program entry
run ; Label run
        MOV r0, #0xFFFFFFFE ; Lower word 1: 0xFFFFFFFE
        MOV r1, #0x00000005 ; Upper word 1: 5
        MOV r2, #0x00000004 ; Lower word 2: 4
        MOV r3, #0x00000002 ; Upper word 2: 2
        ADDS r0, r0, r2 ; Lower sum: 0x00000002, sets Carry flag C=1
        ADC r1, r1, r3 ; Upper sum: 5 + 2 + 1 = 8 (0x00000008)
        SUBS r4, r0, #0x00000010 ; Subtract 16 from lower word, checks borrow
        SBC r5, r1, #0 ; Subtract borrow from upper word
halt B halt ; Loop forever
        END ; Source termination
labs.solutionExplanation: ADDS writes arithmetic status to CPSR; ADC reads the carry flag to complete 64-bit addition; SUBS/SBC perform the corresponding multi-word subtraction.

labs.title: Load/Store & Addressing Modes Lab
labs.syllabusTopic: Load/store instructions, pre/post indexed addressing modes, byte/halfword transfers
labs.objective: Master ARM addressing modes: offset addressing [Rn, #k], pre-indexed writeback [Rn, #k]!, post-indexed [Rn], #k, scaled register offset, and byte/halfword transfers (LDRB, STRB, LDRH, STRH).
labs.problemStatement: Write an ARM assembly routine that reads a word from memory starting at 0x1000, doubles the value, and stores the updated word to destination memory 0x2000 using post-indexed reading and pre-indexed writeback storing.
labs.starterCode:
AREA AddressingLab, CODE, READONLY ; Declare code area
        ENTRY ; Entry point
start ; Start label
        MOV r0, #0x1000 ; Source buffer base pointer
        MOV r1, #0x2000 ; Destination buffer base pointer
        MOV r2, #42 ; Value to write into test memory
        STR r2, [r0] ; Store test value at source address
        LDR r3, [r0], #4 ; Post-indexed load: r3=[r0], then r0=r0+4
        ADD r3, r3, r3 ; Double loaded value (r3 = 42 * 2 = 84)
        STR r3, [r1, #4]! ; Pre-indexed store: r1=r1+4, then [r1]=r3
stop B stop ; Halt
        END ; End of file
labs.expectedState: R0 advances to 0x1004; R1 advances to 0x2004; Memory at 0x1000 holds 42; Memory at 0x2004 holds 84.
labs.boundaryCase: Non-word-aligned addresses (e.g. 0x1001 for a word transfer) cause data rotation on classic ARM7 or Alignment Abort exception on Cortex cores.
labs.hardwareNote: Browser memory model enforces 4-byte word alignment; ARM7 hardware rotates unaligned word reads based on address bits [1:0].
labs.checkpoint: Verify that R0 advances by 4 after load and R1 advances by 4 before store.
labs.solutionCode:
AREA ArrayCopy, CODE, READONLY ; Define code area
        ENTRY ; Program entry
main ; Entry point
        MOV r0, #0x1000 ; Source base pointer
        MOV r1, #0x2000 ; Destination base pointer
        MOV r2, #10 ; Element 1 value
        STR r2, [r0, #0] ; Store element 1
        MOV r2, #20 ; Element 2 value
        STR r2, [r0, #4] ; Store element 2
        LDR r3, [r0], #4 ; Load element 1, advance r0 to 0x1004
        STR r3, [r1], #4 ; Store element 1, advance r1 to 0x2004
        LDR r3, [r0], #4 ; Load element 2, advance r0 to 0x1008
        STR r3, [r1], #4 ; Store element 2, advance r1 to 0x2008
spin B spin ; Halt
        END ; File end
labs.solutionExplanation: Post-indexed addressing [r0], #4 transfers the current word then increments the pointer; pre-indexed writeback [r1, #4]! updates the base register before the write.

labs.title: Control Flow, Loops, Branches & Jump Tables Lab
labs.syllabusTopic: Control flow, loops, branches, condition codes, jump tables
labs.objective: Construct structured loops (while/for/do-while), multi-way decision trees with condition codes, and efficient jump tables using PC modification for command dispatch.
labs.problemStatement: Implement a command dispatcher that takes an opcode (0, 1, or 2) in R0, checks bounds (range 0–2), uses branching to execute handle_add (opcode 0: R3 = R1 + R2), handle_sub (opcode 1: R3 = R1 - R2), or handle_and (opcode 2: R3 = R1 AND R2), returning 0xFFFFFFFF for invalid opcodes.
labs.starterCode:
AREA JumpTableLab, CODE, READONLY ; Declare code area
        ENTRY ; Program entry
start ; Main entry
        MOV r0, #1 ; Test opcode: 1 (subtract command)
        MOV r1, #50 ; Operand 1 = 50
        MOV r2, #20 ; Operand 2 = 20
        CMP r0, #2 ; Verify opcode is within valid range (0..2)
        BHI invalid ; Branch if unsigned higher than maximum opcode
        CMP r0, #0 ; Check for opcode 0
        BEQ handle_add ; Jump to addition handler
        CMP r0, #1 ; Check for opcode 1
        BEQ handle_sub ; Jump to subtraction handler
        B handle_and ; Opcode 2 falls through to bitwise AND handler
handle_add ; Addition handler label
        ADD r3, r1, r2 ; r3 = 50 + 20 = 70
        B done ; Complete dispatch
handle_sub ; Subtraction handler label
        SUB r3, r1, r2 ; r3 = 50 - 20 = 30
        B done ; Complete dispatch
handle_and ; Bitwise AND handler label
        AND r3, r1, r2 ; r3 = 50 AND 20
        B done ; Complete dispatch

labs.problemStatement: Model address decoding for a system with 64 KB ROM at 0x00000000-0x0000FFFF, 128 KB SRAM at 0x40000000-0x4001FFFF, and 4 KB MMIO at 0xE0000000-0xE0000FFF. Write a Python decoder model that verifies chip-select lines CS_ROM, CS_SRAM, CS_MMIO and flags unmapped access.
labs.starterCode:
# Address decoding model for 32-bit microprocessor bus
def decode_address(address):  # Function to decode address
    cs_rom = (address >= 0x00000000) and (address <= 0x0000FFFF)  # 64 KB Flash ROM
    cs_sram = (address >= 0x40000000) and (address <= 0x4001FFFF)  # 128 KB SRAM
    cs_mmio = (address >= 0xE0000000) and (address <= 0xE0000FFF)  # 4 KB MMIO registers
    if cs_rom:  # Check ROM range
        return "CS_ROM"  # Return ROM chip select
    elif cs_sram:  # Check SRAM range
        return "CS_SRAM"  # Return SRAM chip select
    elif cs_mmio:  # Check MMIO range
        return "CS_MMIO"  # Return MMIO chip select
    else:  # Unmapped space
        return "BUS_ERROR"  # Return unmapped error
# Test address range verification
for test_addr in [0x00001000, 0x40005000, 0xE0000020, 0x20000000]:  # Test addresses
    print(f"{hex(test_addr)} -> {decode_address(test_addr)}")  # Print decoded result
labs.boundaryCase: Accessing 0x00010000 (just 1 byte past 64 KB ROM) must return BUS_ERROR, preventing memory overrun.
labs.hardwareNote: In physical hardware, 74LS138 decoders or FPGA logic implement these Boolean equations; incomplete decoding causes address aliasing where one device mirrors across multiple address ranges.
labs.checkpoint: Verify that valid ranges assert exactly one chip select and unmapped addresses trigger BUS_ERROR.
labs.solutionCode:
# Full address decoding verification
def check_memory_space(addr):  # Function to inspect memory space
    # Decode upper address bits [31:16]
    upper = addr >> 16  # Extract upper 16 bits
    if upper == 0x0000:  # ROM region 0x0000xxxx
        return "FLASH_ROM_SELECTED"  # Flash ROM selected
    elif 0x4000 <= upper <= 0x4001:  # SRAM region 0x4000xxxx-0x4001xxxx
        return "SRAM_SELECTED"  # SRAM selected
    elif upper == 0xE000:  # MMIO region 0xE000xxxx
        return "PERIPHERAL_SELECTED"  # Peripheral selected
    return "ILLEGAL_ADDRESS_FAULT"  # Unmapped access

print(check_memory_space(0x40001234))  # Test SRAM address
labs.solutionExplanation: The address decoder slices the top address bits to produce mutual exclusive chip select assertions and traps invalid accesses.

labs.title: Bus Transactions & System Timing Lab
labs.syllabusTopic: System timing, bus transactions, setup/hold times, wait state calculations
labs.objective: Analyze bus read and write cycles, compute required wait states based on clock period and memory access time (tACC), and verify setup and hold timing margins.
labs.problemStatement: A 50 MHz ARM processor has a clock cycle period T_cyc = 20 ns. External memory has an access time t_ACC = 75 ns. Write a timing model to calculate required wait states N_wait = ceil((t_ACC - T_cyc) / T_cyc) and simulate the bus cycle phases (Address, Wait States, Data Latch).
labs.starterCode:
# Bus timing and wait state calculator
import math  # Math utility for ceiling function

clock_freq_mhz = 50.0  # CPU clock frequency in MHz
t_cyc_ns = 1000.0 / clock_freq_mhz  # Clock cycle period = 20.0 ns
t_acc_ns = 75.0  # External memory access time = 75.0 ns

# Compute wait states required beyond 1 base cycle
wait_states = math.ceil((t_acc_ns - t_cyc_ns) / t_cyc_ns)  # ceil((75-20)/20) = 3
total_cycles = 1 + wait_states + 1  # Address phase (1) + Wait (3) + Latch (1)
total_time_ns = total_cycles * t_cyc_ns  # Total bus cycle duration

print(f"Clock period: {t_cyc_ns} ns")  # Output period
print(f"Wait states required: {wait_states}")  # Output wait states
print(f"Total bus cycle duration: {total_time_ns} ns")  # Output total duration
labs.expectedState: Clock period = 20.0 ns; Wait states = 3; Total bus cycles = 5; Total duration = 100.0 ns (satisfies 75 ns t_ACC with 25 ns margin).
labs.boundaryCase: Configuring 0 wait states on a 75 ns memory causes setup time violation and data corruption on the read data bus.
labs.hardwareNote: Physical boards require oscilloscope / logic analyzer verification of t_AS, t_ACC, and t_H; memory controllers insert hardware wait states by pulling the nWAIT / READY line low.
labs.checkpoint: Calculate wait states for a 100 MHz CPU with 45 ns memory and verify total transaction duration.
labs.solutionCode:
# Bus transaction phase simulation
def simulate_bus_read(clock_mhz, mem_access_ns):  # Calculate transaction phases
    t_clk = 1000.0 / clock_mhz  # Clock cycle in ns
    n_wait = max(0, int((mem_access_ns - t_clk + t_clk - 1) // t_clk))  # Integer ceil
    phases = ["T1: ADDRESS_DRIVE"]  # Address drive phase
    for i in range(n_wait):  # Insert required wait states
        phases.append(f"TW{i+1}: WAIT_STATE")  # Wait state insertion
    phases.append("T2: DATA_LATCH")  # Data latch phase
    return n_wait, (len(phases) * t_clk), phases  # Return wait count, duration, log

wait_count, duration, log = simulate_bus_read(50, 75)  # Run simulation for 50MHz / 75ns
print(f"Wait count: {wait_count}, Duration: {duration} ns")  # Print timing results
labs.solutionExplanation: The processor extends the bus cycle by inserting wait states (TW) until the memory device's access time requirement is met before latching data.

labs.objective: Understand SRAM (static latch) vs DRAM (capacitor storage) interfacing, row/column address multiplexing (RAS/CAS), and periodic refresh scheduling within 64 ms retention limits.
labs.problemStatement: Model a DRAM memory controller that decodes a 32-bit physical address into Bank, Row, and Column addresses, and schedules refresh operations every 7.81 microseconds across 8192 rows (64 ms total retention).

# DRAM row/column decoding and refresh timing model
TOTAL_ROWS = 8192  # 8192 rows in DRAM array
RETENTION_TIME_MS = 64.0  # Maximum retention time = 64 ms
REFRESH_INTERVAL_US = (RETENTION_TIME_MS * 1000.0) / TOTAL_ROWS  # 7.8125 us

def decode_dram_addr(phys_addr):  # Decode physical address to DRAM coordinates
    col = phys_addr & 0x3FF  # 10 bits column address (bits 9:0)
    row = (phys_addr >> 10) & 0x1FFF  # 13 bits row address (bits 22:10)
    bank = (phys_addr >> 23) & 0x3  # 2 bits bank address (bits 24:23)
    return bank, row, col  # Return bank, row, and column

bank, row, col = decode_dram_addr(0x00A12340)  # Test address
print(f"Bank: {bank}, Row: {row}, Col: {col}")  # Print decoded components
print(f"Refresh interval: {REFRESH_INTERVAL_US:.2f} us per row")  # Print refresh rate
labs.expectedState: For address 0x00A12340: Bank = 1, Row = 2098, Col = 832; Refresh interval = 7.81 us per row.
labs.boundaryCase: Missing a refresh cycle due to continuous bus transactions causes capacitive discharge and bit corruption in dynamic cells.
labs.hardwareNote: SRAM interfaces directly with static chip-select and write-enable lines; DRAM controllers require specialized auto-refresh counters, row precharge (tRP), and CAS latency (CL) state machines.
labs.checkpoint: Verify that 8192 rows refreshed at 7.8125 us intervals complete a full refresh cycle within 64 ms.
labs.solutionCode:
# DRAM memory controller state machine simulation
def process_dram_request(is_page_hit):  # Calculate latency based on page status
    if is_page_hit:  # Open row page hit
        return 2  # CAS Latency only: 2 cycles
    else:  # Row page miss
        return 6  # Precharge (2) + Activate (2) + CAS Latency (2) = 6 cycles

print(f"Page hit latency: {process_dram_request(True)} cycles")  # Test page hit
print(f"Page miss latency: {process_dram_request(False)} cycles")  # Test page miss
labs.solutionExplanation: DRAM multiplexes addresses on shared pins using RAS# and CAS# strobes; open row page hits execute with low latency while page misses require precharge and activate cycles.

start ; Entry point
        MOV r0, #4 ; Compute factorial of 4 (4! = 24)

stop B stop ; Halt when finished

factorial ; Subroutine entry
        PUSH {r4, lr} ; Save callee register r4 and return address lr
        MOV r4, r0 ; Save current argument n in r4
        CMP r0, #1 ; Test for base case n <= 1

        POP {r4, pc} ; Restore r4 and return to caller
recurse ; Recursive step label
        SUB r0, r0, #1 ; Set argument = n - 1
        BL factorial ; Recursive call: factorial(n - 1)
        MUL r0, r4, r0 ; Compute n * factorial(n - 1)

        LDMFD sp!, {r4, pc} ; Pop r4 and return
        END ; Source end

; Complete Keil ARM7 stack setup

        ENTRY ; Entry point
Reset ; Reset startup label
        MOV r0, #0x40001000 ; Set base stack address in SRAM
        MOV sp, r0 ; Initialize SP
        MOV r1, #0 ; Clear status
        BX lr ; Branch to main
        END ; End of file

labs.title: Timed Comprehensive Lab Rehearsal
labs.syllabusTopic: Comprehensive lab preparation with a timed multi-part practical exercise
labs.objective: Rehearse a timed, comprehensive 90-minute microprocessor lab problem combining address decoding, peripheral I/O control, interrupt service routine design, stack-safe subroutine calling, and error diagnostics.
labs.problemStatement: Complete the 3-part final lab exam problem: (Part A) Calculate the memory address range for a 32 KB SRAM starting at 0x40000000; (Part B) Write an ARM assembly ISR that reads sensor data at MMIO 0xE0004000, checks against limit 100, and sets alarm bit 0 at GPIO 0xE0028000; (Part C) Wrap the DSP routine in a stack-safe subroutine returning status in R0.
labs.starterCode:
; Part B: ARM assembly final lab exam ISR
SENSOR_ADDR EQU 0xE0004000 ; Memory-mapped sensor address
GPIO_ADDR EQU 0xE0028000 ; Memory-mapped GPIO output address
ALARM_LIMIT EQU 100 ; Sensor alarm threshold

        AREA FinalExamLab, CODE, READONLY ; Declare code area
        EXPORT Exam_ISR ; Export ISR symbol
Exam_ISR ; ISR entry point
        SUB lr, lr, #4 ; Adjust link register for IRQ pipeline
        STMFD sp!, {r0-r3, lr} ; Save working registers and return address
        LDR r0, =SENSOR_ADDR ; Load sensor base address
        LDR r1, [r0] ; Read current sensor reading
        CMP r1, #ALARM_LIMIT ; Compare sensor reading with threshold (100)
        BLE clear_alarm ; If sensor <= 100, clear alarm
        LDR r2, =GPIO_ADDR ; Load GPIO base address
        MOV r3, #0x01 ; Alarm bit mask (bit 0 = HIGH)
        STR r3, [r2] ; Turn ON alarm LED on GPIO
        B isr_done ; Finish ISR
clear_alarm ; Clear alarm label
        LDR r2, =GPIO_ADDR ; Load GPIO base address
        MOV r3, #0x00 ; Clear alarm bit
        STR r3, [r2] ; Turn OFF alarm LED
isr_done ; ISR completion label
        LDMFD sp!, {r0-r3, pc}^ ; Restore registers and return atomically
        END ; End of exam assembly source
labs.expectedState: Sensor reading > 100 turns on GPIO bit 0; Sensor reading <= 100 turns off GPIO bit 0; Part A address range: 0x40000000 to 0x40007FFF (32 KB = 32768 bytes).
labs.boundaryCase: Sensor reading exactly equal to 100 must not trigger alarm (BLE branch); stack unbalance in ISR will cause CPU crash on return.
labs.hardwareNote: Full lab exam on real hardware is evaluated under Keil uVision with target board logic analyzer and oscilloscope verification.
labs.checkpoint: Verify all 3 parts: Part A address math, Part B ISR alarm control, and Part C stack-safe calling.
labs.solutionCode:
; Final lab exam complete solution
        AREA ExamComplete, CODE, READONLY ; Code area
        ENTRY ; Entry point
Start_Exam ; Exam entry label
        MOV r0, #105 ; Test sensor value = 105 (>100)
        MOV r1, #0x5000 ; Simulated GPIO address
        CMP r0, #100 ; Test threshold
        MOVGT r2, #1 ; Alarm = ON if > 100
        MOVLE r2, #0 ; Alarm = OFF if <= 100
        STR r2, [r1] ; Store to GPIO
stop_exam B stop_exam ; Halt
        END ; End of solution
labs.solutionExplanation: The comprehensive exam solution integrates conditional testing, memory-mapped I/O access, and atomic stack preservation under strict timing requirements.

title: ARM Assembly Programming
blurb: Write, trace, and debug ARM assembly using instructions, memory addressing, branches, stacks, functions, and exceptions.
description: A practical ARM assembly course focused on writing, tracing, and debugging ARMASM programs.

beginner: Instructions Part 1: syntax, MOV/MVN, memory addressing, barrel shifter
intermediate: Instructions Part 2: flags, comparisons, data processing, control flow, stacks
Functions: register saving and parameter passing
Exceptions: entry, vectors, priorities and SVC

lessons.title: ARMASM program structure & directives
lessons.explanation: Practice building a minimal ARMASM file: define the code area, mark the entry point, create aliases or constants, execute instructions, and end the source.
examples:
AREA RESET, CODE, READONLY
ENTRY
counter RN 0 ; Alias register r0 as counter
limit   EQU 5 ; Define symbolic constant limit
        MOV counter, #0 ; Initialize counter to 0
stop    B stop ; Loop forever
END
commonMistakes: Treating assembler directives such as AREA or EQU as instructions executed by the ARM core.
lessons.explain: Practice building a minimal ARMASM file: define the code area, mark the entry point, create aliases or constants, execute instructions, and end the source.

lessons.title: MOV, MVN & immediate operands
lessons.explanation: Practice loading immediate values, copying register values, and producing a bitwise complement with MOV and MVN.
examples:
AREA RESET, CODE, READONLY
ENTRY
        MOV r0, #17 ; Load immediate value 17 into r0
        MOV r1, r0 ; Copy r0 into r1
        MVN r2, r1 ; Bitwise NOT of r1 into r2
END
commonMistakes: Reading MOV r0, r1 as copying r0 into r1.
lessons.explain: Practice loading immediate values, copying register values, and producing a bitwise complement with MOV and MVN.

lessons.title: LDR/STR & addressing practice
lessons.explanation: Practice loading and storing words, bytes, and halfwords while calculating base-plus-offset, pre-indexed, and post-indexed addresses.
examples:
AREA RESET, CODE, READONLY
ENTRY
        MOV r2, #0x1000 ; Base pointer address
        MOV r0, #17 ; Initial test value 17
        STR r0, [r2] ; Store word to memory
        MOV r0, #23 ; Second test value 23
        STR r0, [r2, #4] ; Store word with offset 4
        LDR r1, [r2] ; Load word from base
        LDR r3, [r2, #4] ; Load word from offset 4
        STR r3, [r2, #8] ; Store word to offset 8
        LDR r4, [r2], #4 ; Post-indexed load and advance pointer
END
commonMistakes: Confusing the address in the base register with the data loaded from memory.
lessons.explain: Practice loading and storing words, bytes, and halfwords while calculating base-plus-offset, pre-indexed, and post-indexed addresses.

lessons.title: Shift practice: LSL, LSR, ASR & ROR
objectives: Combine a shift with a data-processing instruction
lessons.explanation: Practice tracing left shifts, logical right shifts, arithmetic right shifts, and rotates, including a shifted Operand2 inside another instruction.
examples:
AREA RESET, CODE, READONLY
ENTRY
        MOV r0, #7 ; Load value 7
        MOV r1, r0, LSL #1 ; Shift left by 1 (multiply by 2)
        MOV r2, r1, LSR #2 ; Shift right by 2 (divide by 4)
        ADD r3, r0, r0, LSL #4 ; Multiply by 16 and add r0
END
commonMistakes: Assuming LSR and ASR are identical for values whose top bit is 1.
lessons.explain: Practice tracing left shifts, logical right shifts, arithmetic right shifts, and rotates, including a shifted Operand2 inside another instruction.

lessons.title: Flag-setting practice with the S suffix
objectives: Trace N, Z, C, and V
Use the S suffix to update flags
Separate signed overflow from unsigned carry
lessons.explanation: Practice instructions that update CPSR flags and trace the resulting N, Z, C, and V values.
examples:
AREA RESET, CODE, READONLY
ENTRY
        MOV  r0, #5 ; Set initial value 5
        SUBS r1, r0, #5 ; Subtract 5 and update flags (Z=1)
        MOVS r2, #-1 ; Move -1 and update flags (N=1)
END
commonMistakes: Treating C and V as the same condition.
lessons.explain: Practice instructions that update CPSR flags and trace the resulting N, Z, C, and V values.

lessons.title: CMP, TST & conditional execution practice
objectives: Use comparison instructions to set flags
Choose a condition code from flag results
lessons.explanation: Practice setting flags with comparison or test instructions, then choosing the correct conditional instruction or branch.
examples:
AREA RESET, CODE, READONLY
ENTRY
        MOV r0, #2 ; Load test value 2
        CMP r0, #2 ; Compare r0 with 2 (sets Z=1)
        MOVEQ r1, #1 ; Move 1 if equal (executed)
        MOVNE r1, #0 ; Move 0 if not equal (skipped)
        TST r0, #2 ; Bitwise test bit 1
END
commonMistakes: Expecting CMP to store a normal subtraction result.
lessons.explain: Practice setting flags with comparison or test instructions, then choosing the correct conditional instruction or branch.

lessons.title: Bit-manipulation practice
lessons.explanation: Practice using AND, ORR, EOR, and BIC with masks to keep, set, toggle, or clear selected bits.
examples:
AREA RESET, CODE, READONLY
ENTRY
        MOV r0, #0x0F ; Load bit mask 0x0F
        MOV r1, #0x03 ; Load bit mask 0x03
        AND r2, r0, r1 ; Bitwise AND: 0x03
        ORR r3, r0, #0x10 ; Bitwise OR: 0x1F
        EOR r4, r0, r1 ; Bitwise XOR: 0x0C
        BIC r5, r0, #0x03 ; Bit clear lower 2 bits: 0x0C
END
commonMistakes: Using arithmetic intuition for bit masks instead of tracing each bit position.
lessons.explain: Practice using AND, ORR, EOR, and BIC with masks to keep, set, toggle, or clear selected bits.

lessons.title: Arithmetic instruction practice
lessons.explanation: Practice three-operand arithmetic with ADD, ADC, SUB, SBC, RSB, and RSC, including carry-aware and reverse subtraction cases.
examples:
AREA RESET, CODE, READONLY
ENTRY
        MOV r1, #9 ; Load operand 1
        MOV r2, #4 ; Load operand 2
        ADD r0, r1, r2 ; Add: 9 + 4 = 13
        SUB r3, r1, r2 ; Subtract: 9 - 4 = 5
        RSB r4, r1, r2 ; Reverse subtract: 4 - 9 = -5
END
commonMistakes: Applying normal SUB operand order to RSB.
lessons.explain: Practice three-operand arithmetic with ADD, ADC, SUB, SBC, RSB, and RSC, including carry-aware and reverse subtraction cases.

lessons.title: Branch, if/else & loop practice
lessons.explanation: Practice labels, conditional branches, if/else control flow, and loops by tracing the program counter and loop state.
examples:
AREA RESET, CODE, READONLY
ENTRY
j       RN 0 ; Alias register r0 as loop counter j
        MOV j, #3 ; Initialize counter j to 3
loop    CMP j, #0 ; Compare j with 0
        BLT done ; Exit loop when j < 0
        SUB j, j, #1 ; Decrement counter
        B loop ; Repeat loop
done    B done ; Halt when loop finishes
END
commonMistakes: Forgetting that a loop must modify the state used by its termination condition.
lessons.explain: Practice labels, conditional branches, if/else control flow, and loops by tracing the program counter and loop state.

lessons.title: Stack & multiple-register transfer practice
lessons.explanation: Practice LDM/STM and PUSH/POP while tracing SP and the memory addresses used by each transfer.
examples:
AREA RESET, CODE, READONLY
ENTRY
        LDR r3, =0x11111111 ; Load literal value 1
        LDR r4, =0x22222222 ; Load literal value 2
        PUSH {r3, r4} ; Push r3 and r4 onto stack
        POP  {r5, r6} ; Pop from stack into r5 and r6
END
commonMistakes: Assuming textual register-list order controls memory ordering.
lessons.explain: Practice LDM/STM and PUSH/POP while tracing SP and the memory addresses used by each transfer.

lessons.title: Subroutine & parameter-passing practice
objectives: Call and return from a subroutine
Compare register, memory-block, and stack parameter passing
lessons.explanation: Practice BL, BX LR, register preservation, and parameter passing by tracing calls and returns.
examples:
AREA RESET, CODE, READONLY
ENTRY
main    MOV r0, #5 ; Main function argument
        BL double ; Branch with link to subroutine
        B stop ; Halt execution

double  PUSH {r1} ; Save caller register r1
        ADD r1, r0, r0 ; Double value in r0
        MOV r0, r1 ; Store return value in r0
        POP {r1} ; Restore caller register r1
        BX lr ; Return to caller
stop    B stop ; Spin loop
END
commonMistakes: Calling another function without protecting LR when the current function still needs its own return address.
lessons.explain: Practice BL, BX LR, register preservation, and parameter passing by tracing calls and returns.

lessons.title: Exception-vector & handler practice
objectives: Trace major classic ARM exception types
lessons.explanation: Practice reading the classic ARM vector table and tracing how control reaches and returns from reset, SVC, IRQ, FIQ, and abort handlers.
examples:
0x00  Reset ; Hardware reset entry point
0x04  Undefined instruction ; Undefined instruction trap
0x08  SVC ; Supervisor call software interrupt
0x0C  Prefetch abort ; Instruction fetch memory fault
0x10  Data abort ; Data access memory fault
0x18  IRQ ; Standard priority hardware interrupt
0x1C  FIQ ; Fast priority hardware interrupt
commonMistakes: Using the same unadjusted LR return sequence for every exception type.
lessons.explain: Practice reading the classic ARM vector table and tracing how control reaches and returns from reset, SVC, IRQ, FIQ, and abort handlers.

quiz.q: AREA, ENTRY, EQU, and END are primarily:
quiz.explanation: AREA organizes a section, ENTRY marks an entry point, EQU defines a constant, and END ends the source. These direct the assembler rather than perform CPU calculations.

quiz.q: For a typical three-operand ARM data-processing instruction, the first register is usually:
quiz.explanation: In ADD r0, r1, r2, r0 receives the result while r1 and r2 supply values. Read the operands from destination to sources.
MOV r0, r1 reads r1 and writes its value into r0. r1 is unchanged.

options: The bitwise complement of its operand
quiz.explanation: MVN flips every bit of the source. In a 32-bit register, MVN applied to 0 gives 0xFFFFFFFF, not 1.
RSB reverses the usual SUB order: RSB r0, r1, r2 stores r2 minus r1 in r0.

options: A carry from a previous arithmetic step must be included
quiz.explanation: ADC computes operand1 + operand2 + C. This lets the carry from a low-word addition feed a high-word addition.
BIC computes operand1 AND NOT operand2. A 1 in the mask therefore clears the corresponding destination bit.
EOR sets a result bit when the two corresponding input bits differ; equal bits produce 0.

quiz.q: ASR differs from LSR because ASR:
options: Preserves the sign bit when shifting right
quiz.explanation: ASR replicates the top/sign bit while shifting right. LSR shifts zeros into the high positions.

options: Shift an operand as part of another data-processing instruction
quiz.explanation: ADD r0, r1, r2, LSL #2 shifts r2 left by two before adding it to r1. The shifted value need not be stored in a separate register.

quiz.q: The Z flag is set when the relevant result is:
quiz.explanation: Z is 1 when the flag-setting operation produces zero. A plain instruction without S usually leaves these flags unchanged.
V indicates that the mathematical signed result cannot fit in a signed 32-bit value. It is different from unsigned carry C.

options: Updates condition flags based on a subtraction-like comparison
quiz.explanation: CMP uses a subtraction to set NZCV but discards the arithmetic result. It does not overwrite either compared register.

quiz.q: TST primarily uses which logical operation for flag testing?
quiz.explanation: TST calculates a bitwise AND for the flags without saving that AND result in a destination register.

options: Condition flags and a condition code
quiz.explanation: The condition suffix reads flags set earlier. BEQ tests Z=1; BLT tests N different from V for a signed comparison.

quiz.q: A do-while style loop differs from a while loop because its body:
quiz.explanation: A do-while style loop places its test after the body, so the body runs at least once. A while style loop can skip the body when its first test fails.

options: Load data from memory into a register
quiz.explanation: LDR reads the word at an effective memory address and places it in the destination register. STR transfers a register value in the opposite direction.

options: Uses the current base address, then updates the base
Updates the base before the access only
quiz.explanation: LDR r0, [r1], #4 loads using the old address in r1, then increases r1 by four. The offset is outside the brackets.
PUSH preserves register values in memory on the stack and adjusts SP. It is useful before a subroutine changes values the caller needs.

quiz.q: In the stack convention shown in the lectures, the stack grows toward:
quiz.explanation: In the full descending convention, reserving stack space decreases SP; releasing it increases SP. Lower memory addresses hold newer stack entries.

quiz.q: BL does what in addition to branching?
options: Saves a return address in LR
quiz.explanation: BL saves the address of the instruction after the call in LR before transferring control. A nested call must preserve a needed earlier LR.

quiz.q: A simple subroutine commonly returns with:
quiz.explanation: BX LR branches to the saved return address. LR must still hold the intended return address for this to work.

quiz.q: On classic ARM exception entry, CPSR is copied into:
quiz.explanation: Classic ARM exception entry saves the old CPSR in the target mode SPSR so the handler can later restore the interrupted status. The tracer does not model exception entry.

options: Request a privileged software service by raising a software exception
quiz.explanation: SVC deliberately raises a software exception to request a supervisor service. It is not an ordinary BL subroutine call; handling depends on the execution environment.
